messages.content: my cousin is coming for a holiday meal. last year we made rice together, and i keep thinking we should do the same thing again.
you can ask whether they would enjoy that again or want to try something different. an old plan can be a good idea without having to become the only choice.
i want the time together more than any specific food.
then say that first. you could write: i would like us to cook together again. would you like rice as before, or something else this time?
they ask what i want. i am happy with rice, but i want them to have a choice too.
you could reply: i would enjoy making rice again. is there something you would rather make together?
what if they choose soup instead?
if soup works for you, you can choose that and still keep the part you care about: cooking together. the food can change, and you can still have time together in the kitchen.
say it simply.
the food can change, and you can still have time together in the kitchen.
write the short reply for choosing soup.
soup sounds good. i am happy we can cook together again.
i put four coins on a table. my brother takes one, then gives it back. how many are on the table now?
if he puts that coin back on the table and nothing else changes, there are four again.
he gives it back to my hand, not the table.
then there are three on the table and one in your hand. giving it back to you does not always mean putting it in its old place.
how many coins do i have in both places together?
if all four are yours, you have four coins: three on the table and one in your hand.
use all four are mine in a short answer.
if all four are yours, you have four.
now i put the one in my hand into a container. do i have fewer coins?
no. you changed the place of one coin. there are still four of your coins, with three on the table and one in the container.
write a short explanation of the difference between number and place.
moving a coin changes where it is. it does not by itself change how many coins there are.
i want a story where a child waits for someone to finish talking before asking a question. keep it kind, without saying the child is wrong to ask.

a child listens while her aunt gives the first example of a game. she thinks of a question and waits until the example is over. then she asks why one person can move only one object. her aunt says that the next person needs to play after that. the child asks if they can try it slowly. they put the objects on the table and begin together.
make the story simple.
a child listens while her aunt gives an example of a game. after the example, she asks a question. her aunt answers, then they try the game slowly together.
does waiting mean she must forget her question?
no. she can remember it or keep a short note while listening. waiting for a good place to ask is different from not asking at all.
what if she needs the answer to understand the example?
then she can ask now: could you explain that first part before we go on? understanding the idea is important too.
give just the question.
could you explain that first part before we go on?
my friend sent a picture of a station. can i know they are at the station now?
not from that alone. they might have taken the picture before, or someone else might have sent it to them. ask if you need to know where they are now.
what could i ask without making it sound like i do not believe them?
are you at the station now, or is this from another time?
they say they took it yesterday and are home now. write a reply asking about yesterday.
what were you doing at the station yesterday?
if they say they met a cousin there, can i write that they rode a train?
not unless they say that too. they could meet a person at the station without riding on a train themselves.
say it simply.
they could meet a person at the station without riding on a train themselves. you do not know that part yet.
write a question asking about that detail.
did you take a train too, or did you just meet your cousin there?
say my last request simply.
write a question asking whether they rode a train or only met their cousin.
write a story where a child looks at his hands in a mirror and asks what he is seeing. do not make up a new fact about his body.

a child holds one hand up in front of a mirror. he looks at the hand in the glass and asks whether there is another child behind it. his sister says that the picture moves when he moves. he puts his hand down, then holds it up again. the hand in the mirror does the same. he has a smile and asks whether he can make a face and see that too.
use has a smile in the last part.
he has a smile and asks whether he can make a face and see that too.
does the story say he has more hands after looking in the mirror?
no. he still has the same hands. the mirror helps him see the hand he is holding up.
say it simply.
no. looking in a mirror does not add more hands to his body.
use helps in one sentence.
the mirror helps him see the hand he is holding up.
write a last sentence where he tries with both hands.
he holds up both hands and watches what happens in the mirror.
i am going to a village for a week. does that mean i am moving there to live?
not by itself. going for a week sounds like a visit, unless you give more information. moving there to live would be a different plan.
write a message to my friend that keeps it as a visit.
i will visit the village for a week, then come home.
now make it clear i do not know the return day yet.
i will visit the village for about a week, but i have not chosen the return day yet.
about is in the list. does it change a week to a number of days for sure?
no. about a week leaves the day open. it does not give a specific number of days for sure.
answer simply.
no. about a week is not a sure number of days.
what can i ask the person i will stay with?
would a visit of about a week work for you, or would you like a shorter visit?
use like in a short question.
would you like a visit of about a week or a shorter one?
i stopped the music after one song because i wanted quiet. my friend thought i did not like the song.
you can explain the difference: i liked the song. i just want quiet now. a change in what you want next does not always change what you liked before.
say my first message simply.
i stopped the music after one song because i wanted quiet. my friend thought i did not like the song.
write a kind reply without saying my friend was wrong to ask.
i did like it, thank you. i just wanted a little quiet after that song.
ask my last request simply.
write a kind reply without saying my friend was wrong to ask.
what if i want another song later?
you can want quiet now and still want music later.
use want in a short answer.
you can want quiet now and another song later.
put that into one short message.
i liked the song. i want quiet for now, but i may play more music later.
my child drew me at a desk because i often work there. i want to tell them i like the picture without saying work is all i do.
you can thank them for the part they saw: i like how you drew my desk. that is where i do some of my work.
can you ask them about another part of the picture?
what made you choose the window next to the desk?
they say it is because i always look outside. i do look outside sometimes, but not always.
you could say: i do like looking outside sometimes. i also look at my work and talk with you. always is a big word for every moment.
is it okay to leave the picture as it is?
yes. a picture can show one part of your day. it does not have to show everything you do.
say it simply.
yes. a picture does not have to show every part of a day.
write a short reply that keeps the child idea.
i like the window next to my desk. looking outside is one part of my day that you saw.
use keeps, kept, and keeping in a short story about a card.
a woman keeps a card inside her book so she can find her place. yesterday, she kept it on the desk while she read. now she is keeping it between the pages again before closing the book.
which part is about yesterday?
she kept it on the desk while she read. kept is the word used for that past part.
what if she leaves it in the book when she is not reading, but takes it out when she reads?
then you could say: she usually keeps it in the book, but takes it out while reading. that gives the general place and the change during reading.
use usually and but.
she usually keeps it in the book, but takes it out while reading.
can you write the whole story about yesterday only?
yesterday, she kept a card in her book before reading. she took it out and put it on the desk while she read. before closing the book, she put the card back between the pages.
does that tell us what she did today?
no. that story is only about yesterday.
say it simply.
no. today is not in that story.
six people work in groups of two. each group writes one answer. how many answers will there be?
six people make three groups of two. if each group writes one answer, there will be three answers.
say it using group of two.
six people make three groups of two. if each group writes one answer, there will be three answers.
now each person writes one answer instead. what changes?
then there are six answers, one from each person. the number changes because the task changed from one answer for a group to one for a person.
can one person still help another after writing their own answer?
yes. writing one answer each does not say that they cannot talk or help. you would need another rule if the work must be done alone.
use another rule in one sentence.
you would need another rule if the work must be done alone.
write a short request that makes the group task clear.
work in groups of two. each group should write one answer together.
my sister wrote good morning, but i only read the message at night. do i have to answer good morning back?
no. you can reply for the time when you are writing, or simply say hello. you can also say you have only just read her message.
write a short reply with no reason i did not give.
hello. i have only just read your message. how was your day?
why not say i was busy all day?
you did not tell me why you read it at night. being busy is one possible reason, but adding it would make up a detail.
can i say sorry for the late reply?
yes, if you want to. you can say it without choosing a reason: sorry for the late reply. i have only just read this.
does late reply mean the message was sent late too?
no. her message was sent in the morning. your reply came later. those are different parts of the conversation.
make a one sentence answer saying when she sent it and when i answered.
she sent the message in the morning, and i answered at night.
ask my last request simply.
write one sentence saying when she sent it and when i answered.
i find it hard to start talking with someone new. i do not need a big plan, just one simple question.
you could ask about something you can both see or do. if you are at a library, for example: have you read anything you enjoyed today?
use today in a simple question.
have you read anything you enjoyed today?
what if i do not know whether they have been reading?
then use a question about the place or what brought them there: do you come to this library often?
i want a school example, not a library example.
what do you like doing after school?
i want an example, not a fact about where i am.
then that question is a made up example for school. it does not say where you are now.
can the other person answer only a few words?
yes. a simple first question gives them a place to start. you can listen and ask one follow up if they want to keep talking.
what if they do not want to talk?
you can leave the conversation there. a kind question does not need a long answer every time.
say it simply.
you can ask a kind question, and the other person can choose to keep the answer short or stop there.
